title: Straw (6 December 1273)
hook: after an experience at Mass he stops writing: all I've written seems like straw

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crucifix in Naples: asked what reward he wanted, Thomas answered, nothing but you. Your line was only you, Lord. What was underneath the thing you wanted? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

A pen goes down on a desk and doesn't get picked up again. That's the whole scene. No fire, no vision on a mountain. As tradition tells it, Thomas Aquinas, in the middle of the third part of the Summa, the great book this whole block has been walking through, goes to Mass one morning in Naples. Something happens there. Afterward he stops writing, and he doesn't start again. His friends are alarmed. One of them, his companion Reginald, keeps asking why. Today's word is the answer Thomas gave him.
screen: `A PEN GOES DOWN.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS AT MASS.` → `REGINALD ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Tradition gives his answer like this. I can't, Reginald. Everything I have written seems to me like straw, compared with what I have seen. In Latin the word is palea: straw, or chaff, the dry husk left over when the grain is gone. Nobody knows what Thomas saw. He didn't describe it. The people who passed the story down didn't claim to know either, and it's better not to fill in the silence for him. What tradition does say is that the Summa was left unfinished. So what does this mean? One easy reading is that his work was worthless, and he finally admitted it. Catholics haven't taken it that way. The Church went on to call him a Doctor of the Church and still teaches from his books. The point is the comparison. Straw next to what he saw. A map is straw next to the mountain. A letter is straw next to the person walking through the door. Thomas himself had written that what we say of God is true, but always falls short of him. Here he seems to have felt that falling short from the inside. Paul says something close, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Some readers notice one more thing. Straw isn't nothing. It's what held the grain while it grew. So Thomas's words may be straw, and still worth carrying. And there's a quiet lesson in the stopping. A man whose mind had hardly ever stopped set the pen down, and let himself rest in something bigger than his work.
screen: `EVERYTHING SEEMS LIKE STRAW.` · `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT HE SAW.` · `STRAW NEXT TO THE MOUNTAIN.` · `STRAW HELD THE GRAIN.` · then, large: `BUT THEN FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest from your work. Settle, and breathe. Notice whatever task is pulling at you right now, the email, the dishes, the deadline. Let it sit on the desk for two minutes. You'll pick it up again. Thomas didn't, but you will. For now, let your hands go loose. Let your work be smaller than you, just for this sit. If you pray, you can rest in God without saying anything at all. The bell holds the time.
Straw. In Latin, palea, the dry husk around the grain. Thomas's word, tradition says, for all he had written, next to what he had seen. Today's word.

Your line: like straw. Today, when your work starts to feel like everything, set it down for five minutes, and remember it holds something bigger than itself. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics tell this story when speaking of Thomas, as a reminder that even the best theology falls short of God; the Summa itself is still studied in seminaries and universities.

notes: The title's date (6 December 1273, feast of Saint Nicholas) comes from tradition via the canonization testimony; per the claims rule it is not repeated in the spoken script. Keeper to confirm the title's date.
Thomas's words paraphrased from the reported Latin ('omnia quae scripsi videntur mihi paleae respectu eorum quae vidi'); confirm. 'Palea' glossed as straw or chaff.
Setting the Mass in Naples and Reginald as the questioner follow the early accounts; confirm.
'The Church went on to call him a Doctor of the Church' — he was canonized in 1323 and declared Doctor in 1567; no dates given in the script. Confirm.
'Straw held the grain' is offered as 'some readers notice'; confirm it is a fair, non-novel reading.
